title: Brass bands, spirituals and revival meetings
summary: No funeral brass bands in Texas; he bluesed up band parts and drew his influence from spirituals heard at camp meetings and played church solos.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Did they ever play any funerals with brass bands over there?

Not in Texas. I don't think that, uh, I don't know of any place in Texas where they ever did that. That's customary in, uh, New Orleans. Uh, here in Louisiana is about the only place I think they ever did in the United States. Uh, uh, this little band, uh, that we had didn't, uh, didn't do much for us, for me, rather, in the way of the jazz field. But, I was sort of, uh, I had ideas of my own. I could hear chords. I could hear harmony. And, I had a pretty good ear and a little talent. And, put them all together. Uh, I guess I might have annoyed the bandmaster a little bit by, uh, sort of, uh, filling in. And, uh, so, uh, kind of bluesing it up a little bit, everything, you know. However, he, uh, used to kind of admire me for doing it. He says, uh, it's not written that way, but it sounds alright. I think that I got my, uh, influence from the spirituals more than anything. If there was ever a revival meeting around, I used to try and get around, sneak around, and listen in to the music as much as I could. And, that seemed to be the thing that came natural to me.
Well, what churches would this be in? What kind? Well, Baptist Methodist or what?

Uh, the spirituals, uh, was, uh, always from the Negroes when they'd have camp meetings. And, uh, revival meetings. However, I used to play in the Christian church in Vernon, Texas. Every Sunday I'd have a little solo worked up. And, uh, but that was a little type, different type of music that was for the choir. Uh, I think that, uh, we'll continue after just a few minutes, huh?
